questions.id: Indefinite integral of cos(x) from 0 to pi/2
questions.solution: The antiderivative of cos(x) is sin(x). Therefore, the indefinite integral of cos(x) dx is sin(x) + C.
questions.explanation: To integrate a function, find its antiderivative. The derivative of sin(x) is cos(x), so the antiderivative of cos(x) is sin(x).
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to choose B (cos(x) + C), which is incorrect because it is not the antiderivative of cos(x).

questions.id: Definite integral of e^x from 1 to 2
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral: ∫e^x dx from x = 1 to x = 2
questions.solution: The antiderivative of e^x is e^x. Evaluate at the limits: (e^2 - e^1) = e^2 - e.
questions.explanation: To evaluate a definite integral, find the antiderivative and then evaluate it at the given limits. The derivative of e^x is itself, so the antiderivative is also e^x.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to choose D (e^2 - 1), which is the difference of the function values at the limits but not the result of evaluating the definite integral.

questions.stem: Evaluate the integral using substitution: ∫(x^2 + 3)^3 dx
questions.explanation: To integrate by substitution, choose a suitable u and find du/dx. Then change the integrand accordingly and integrate with respect to u. Finally, substitute back x^2 + 3 for u.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to forget to multiply by du/dx or to use the wrong power rule when integrating (u)^3.

questions.stem: Evaluate the integral using integration by parts: ∫xe^(2x) dx
questions.explanation: To integrate by parts, choose u and dv/dx such that the product rule can be used to simplify the integral. Integrate dv/dx to get v, then apply the integration by parts formula: ∫udv = uv - ∫vdu.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to integrate e^(2x) incorrectly or to forget to subtract the second part of the integration by parts formula.

questions.id: Integration of a logarithmic function: ∫ln(x) dx
questions.solution: The antiderivative of ln(x) is x ln(x) - x + C. Use integration by parts with u = ln(x), dv/dx = dx/x.
questions.explanation: To integrate a logarithmic function, use integration by parts. Choose u = ln(x) and dv/dx = dx/x to simplify the integral.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to forget to subtract x from the antiderivative of x ln(x), which comes from integrating by parts.

questions.id: Integration of a rational function: ∫(2x + 1)/(x^2 + 2) dx
questions.stem: Evaluate the integral using partial fraction decomposition: ∫(2x + 1)/(x^2 + 2) dx
questions.solution: Decompose into partial fractions: A/(x + √2) + B/(x - √2). Solve for A and B, integrate each term separately.
questions.explanation: To integrate a rational function, decompose it into partial fractions with linear denominators. Then integrate each term using basic integration techniques.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to choose the wrong decomposition or to integrate the resulting terms incorrectly.

questions.id: Integration of a trigonometric substitution: ∫(1 + x^2)^(-1/2) dx
questions.stem: Evaluate the integral using trigonometric substitution: ∫(1 + x^2)^(-1/2) dx
questions.solution: Let x = tan(θ), dx/dθ = sec^2(θ). ∫(1 + x^2)^(-1/2) dx = ∫cos^2(θ)dθ = (1/2)θ + (1/2)sin(θ) + C = arctan(x) + C.
questions.explanation: To integrate a trigonometric substitution, choose an appropriate substitution that simplifies the integrand. In this case, x = tan(θ) leads to cos^2(θ). Integrate with respect to θ and substitute back for x.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to choose the wrong substitution or to integrate the resulting trigonometric function incorrectly.
